- When sentiment is strongly negative (e.g., < -0.5) and forecast is high, reduce forecast by 5–15% to avoid overconfidence in upward moves.
- After a sharp spike in price (e.g., >+10% from prior 7-day avg), model tends to overshoot — cap forecast at 1–2 days above peak, then allow gradual decay.
- If sentiment is mixed or neutral (e.g., -0.3 to 0.3), model often overestimates mean — apply a 3–7% downward bias for 3–5 day horizon.
- When true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days below 30-day moving avg), model tends to lag — adjust forecast to align with 1–2 prior days’ low.
- For 30-day horizon, if sentiment is consistently negative and price is trending down, model often underestimates the drop — add 2–5% downward bias to forecast.
- If sentiment is positive but price is falling, model may misread sentiment — reduce forecast by 3–8% to avoid sentiment-driven overcorrection.
- If true outcome shows sudden drop after a spike, model often fails to recognize the “reset” — apply a 5–10% downward correction to forecast 3–5 days after spike.
